# Personal Statement

During my three years as a community liaison for the Boston Housing Authority, I learned that policy don't exist in a vacuum. I worked with residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to document living conditions in aging public housing units, conducting over 80 interviews about maintenance issues, mold problems, and heating failures during winter months. This experience showed me how federal and state housing policies directly affects the daily lives of vulnerable populations, which is why I want to study public policy. Last year, I helped organize a presentation to the BHA board where residents presented their findings directly, and this led to increased funding for capital repairs in three buildings. Prior to my role at the BHA, I was volunteering at a food bank, which taught me about supply chain issues and how SNAP benefits don't always align with what food banks can actually provide to their clients. The disconnect between policy intent and implementation became clear to me during those years. Additionally, I was involved with the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative's community benefits agreement negotiations, where I observed how marginalized communities can leverage policy tools to ensure that new development benefits existing residents rather than displacing them. These experiences has convinced me that I need formal training in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy to understand the structural barriers that my community faces.

I am particularly interested in your program because of its focus on policy analysis and social equity, and also because Professor James Chen's research on community benefits agreements directly connects to my work at DSNI. Graduate school represents an opportunity for me to deepen my understanding of how to translate community knowledge into effective policy recommendations and advocacy strategies, building on the foundation I've developed through grassroots work. I believe that strong policy requires both technical skills and authentic engagement with affected communities, which your program seems to cultivate through its field placements and practicum requirements. I'm ready to bring my experience and my commitment to public housing and community development to your program.

feedback1:
This is a genuinely strong draft — you have exactly the kind of concrete, verifiable material (specific interview counts, named neighborhoods, a real funding outcome) that makes a personal statement credible rather than generic, and the whole piece stays tightly on-topic from first sentence to last. The core issue to fix before anything else is structural: the first paragraph narrates three experiences (BHA, food bank, DSNI) out of chronological order, jumping backward with "Prior to my role at the BHA" after you've already established a BHA timeline, then tacking on DSNI with a vague "Additionally." Because this paragraph is doing the essay's most important work — showing how your thinking developed — the reader shouldn't have to reconstruct the timeline themselves. Reordering the experiences chronologically (or organizing them explicitly by theme instead of time) will make the growth arc visible rather than making the section read like a list of credentials. Related to this, your real thesis — that these experiences convinced you that you need formal training in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy — doesn't arrive until the very end of the paragraph. Consider surfacing that claim earlier so the anecdotes that follow read as evidence supporting a stated argument, and then let your closing line echo that same claim so the essay feels full-circle rather than ending on the generic "I'm ready to bring my experience and commitment" note.

Once the ordering and framing are sorted out, there are three content-level opportunities that would sharpen the piece further. First, the Professor Chen sentence asserts a connection to his research rather than demonstrating one — given your firsthand DSNI experience, naming a specific idea from his work you want to build on or complicate would make the fit argument much more convincing. Second, your forward-looking vision ("translate community knowledge into effective policy recommendations") is currently generic enough to fit almost any applicant; given how specific your past experience is (mold, heating failures, SNAP misalignment), you have the material to name a concrete future policy question or population focus, which would give the admissions committee a clearer sense of what the degree is for. Third, the program-fit paragraph mentions field placements and practicum requirements but doesn't connect them to a specific gap your grassroots work revealed — naming that gap would make the case for why you need this program, not just any program, airtight.

At the sentence level, there are a few small but real grammar errors worth cleaning up: "policy don't exist" should be "policy doesn't exist," "policies directly affects" should be "policies... affect," and "these experiences has convinced" should be "have convinced." There's also a tense slip ("I was volunteering" should likely be "I volunteered" to match the surrounding simple past). Beyond correctness, the prose would benefit from more sentence-length variety — nearly every sentence in both paragraphs is long and clause-stacked, which creates a monotonous rhythm; a few short, direct sentences placed at moments of emphasis would give the reading more punch. Finally, tighten some repeated words and phrases: "directly" appears three times, "experience(s)" is overused as a noun, and the cluster of "showed me / taught me / became clear to me" could be varied with sharper verbs like *revealed*, *underscored*, or *crystallized*. "Helped organize" also undersells your role in securing real funding outcomes — a stronger verb like *coordinated* or *spearheaded* would match the impact you're describing. None of these are major rewrites, but together they'll make writing that's already substantively strong feel as polished and confident as the experience behind it.

# Personal Statement

Policy doesn't exist in a vacuum. That conviction is what has pushed me toward graduate study in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy, and it took shape gradually, through years of work that revealed the gap between what policy promises and what it delivers.

Before I worked in housing policy, I volunteered at a food bank, where I learned about supply chain issues and saw how SNAP benefits don't always align with what food banks can actually provide to their clients. The disconnect between policy intent and implementation crystallized for me there. It sharpened further during my three years as a community liaison for the Boston Housing Authority. I worked with residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to document living conditions in aging public housing units, conducting over 80 interviews about maintenance issues, mold problems, and heating failures during winter months. State and federal housing policies affect the daily lives of vulnerable populations in ways no memo can capture. Last year, I spearheaded a presentation to the BHA board where residents presented their findings directly, which led to increased funding for capital repairs in three buildings. That outcome mattered. It proved that resident testimony, backed by data, can move institutions. More recently, I worked with the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative on its community benefits agreement negotiations, where I watched marginalized communities leverage policy tools to ensure that new development benefits existing residents rather than displacing them. Together, this work has convinced me that community knowledge alone is not enough. I need formal training to understand the structural barriers my community faces — training that would let me help design accountability mechanisms, such as enforceable maintenance and repair standards, so that housing policy stops failing the tenants it is meant to protect.

I am particularly interested in your program because of its focus on policy analysis and social equity, and because Professor James Chen's research on how community benefits agreements hold up after developers break ground speaks directly to what I saw at DSNI: negotiating the agreement was the easy part; enforcing it afterward was where residents' power was tested. I want to study that enforcement gap and help build monitoring and accountability tools that keep both developers and housing authorities to their commitments — tools that could have made a difference for the tenants I interviewed in Roxbury, whose maintenance requests and mold complaints too often disappeared after they were filed. My grassroots work taught me how to organize residents and document conditions, but not how to rigorously evaluate whether the policies we win actually improve those conditions over time. Your program's field placements and practicum requirements would let me test policy analysis and program evaluation methods against real communities, closing that exact gap. I am ready to bring my history in public housing and community development to that work, and to leave your program with the analytical training I need to turn what residents already know into policy that holds.
feedback2:
# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

This is a strong draft with genuine, compelling experiences that demonstrate real commitment to public policy work. You have clear stories to tell and a genuine connection between your community work and your academic aspirations. However, there are several areas where revision will significantly strengthen your application.

Let me start with grammar and mechanics, since these matter in graduate admissions. In your first sentence, you write "policy don't exist," but "policy" is singular, so it should be "doesn't exist." Later, you write "directly affects," but this should be "directly affect" because the subject is "policies" (plural). Similarly, near the end of the first paragraph, you write "These experiences has convinced me," but "experiences" is plural, so it should be "have convinced." These subject-verb agreement errors are relatively easy fixes, but they do distract admissions readers and suggest you haven't carefully revised your work. I'd recommend reading your statement aloud slowly and checking each verb carefully.

Beyond these technical issues, I want to address the larger structural concern: your statement tries to cover too much ground. You move through four different organizations and roles—the BHA, a food bank, DSNI, and back to the BHA—without deeply developing any single narrative. While each experience teaches you something, the cumulative effect feels scattered rather than building a coherent argument about who you are as a future policy student. Consider this: could you choose one or two experiences that best illustrate your core insight about the gap between policy intent and implementation? The BHA work seems particularly strong because it has a concrete outcome (the presentation that led to funding), and it connects directly to the program you're applying to. You might use that as your anchor and either eliminate the food bank reference or integrate it more briefly as supporting evidence for your broader realization.

The second paragraph assumes too much. You mention Professor James Chen's research on community benefits agreements, but you don't explain why this research matters to you or what specifically draws you to it beyond the fact that it "directly connects" to your work. This feels like you're checking a box rather than making an authentic case. If his research truly excites you, what specific questions or problems does it address? How does it build on insights from your own experience? The more specific you can be about the intellectual substance of what attracts you to the program, the more convincing you'll be. Generic praise for "field placements and practicum requirements" could apply to many programs, so it doesn't really make your case for why this particular program is right for you.

I'd also gently suggest reconsidering the phrase "building on the foundation I've developed through grassroots work." This risks positioning your community experience as merely foundational—something to move beyond rather than something you'll continue to value alongside technical training. Your statement would be stronger if it emphasized how you want to integrate community knowledge with policy analysis rather than moving from one to the other. This distinction matters because it shows admissions committees that you understand the value of both practical and academic expertise.

Finally, your concluding sentence—"I'm ready to bring my experience and my commitment to public housing and community development to your program"—is somewhat generic. Rather than telling the committee you're ready, show them through specific examples what insights you'd bring to classroom discussions or what kinds of projects you're eager to work on. What would you want to study or analyze? Are there particular policy questions or communities you want to focus on?

In revision, I'd encourage you to deepen rather than broaden. Choose your strongest, most specific experiences; cut the elements that feel less central to your core narrative; and use the space you save to explain more precisely what draws you intellectually to this program and what you hope to accomplish there.

feedback1:
This is a strong draft with genuinely compelling raw material — the specificity of your experience (80 interviews, mold and heating documentation, the BHA board presentation that led to real funding, the DSNI negotiations) is exactly what makes a policy statement persuasive, and your vocabulary in this register (community benefits agreements, structural barriers, capital repairs) shows real fluency. The core problem isn't what you have, it's how it's organized and where it's pointing. Fix the structure first, then the smaller language issues, and this will be in excellent shape.

Compounding this, your real organizing insight — "the disconnect between policy intent and implementation" — is buried mid-paragraph as a transitional aside between the food bank and DSNI material, when it should be the thesis that opens the paragraph and that each experience visibly builds on. Right now the three experiences read as a list of credentials rather than a developing argument. Reordering chronologically (or thematically), giving this insight more prominence early on, and considering splitting this into two paragraphs would let the "aha" arrive with the force it deserves rather than sneaking in sideways.

You build a strong case for why you care about housing policy, but you never quite say what you want to do with the degree — what role, what issue area, what concrete goal. # Personal Statement

In a public housing unit in Roxbury, a resident once showed me mold blooming behind a bathroom vent that two winters of maintenance requests had failed to fix. That moment taught me what I now build my work around: policy that looks sound on paper can still fail the people it is meant to serve. The distance between intent and implementation is where the real work of public policy happens. I saw this gap first at a food bank, where I volunteered before joining the Boston Housing Authority. There, I learned that SNAP benefits often did not align with what food banks could realistically stock or distribute, leaving clients caught between a policy designed in one place and a supply chain built in another.

I saw the same gap, at greater scale, during my three years as a community liaison for the Boston Housing Authority. I worked with residents in Roxbury to document living conditions in aging public housing units, conducting more than 80 interviews about maintenance issues, mold, and heating failures during winter months. These interviews showed me how federal and state housing policies shape the daily lives of vulnerable populations, and why I want to study public policy. Last year, I helped organize a presentation to the BHA board where residents shared their findings directly; the board responded with increased funding for capital repairs in three buildings. That outcome confirmed what the food bank had first suggested to me: when policy fails, it usually fails at the level of implementation, and residents who understand that failure firsthand are often best positioned to fix it.

More recently, I saw the reverse dynamic through my involvement with the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative's community benefits agreement negotiations, where marginalized communities used policy tools proactively to ensure that new development benefited existing residents rather than displacing them. Between the BHA and DSNI, I saw both sides of the same problem: policy that fails without community input, and policy that succeeds because of it. These experiences convinced me that I need formal training in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy to address the structural barriers my community faces, and to help design policy that works before residents have to fight to fix it.

Structural barriers like these are exactly what I hope to study further in your program. I am particularly interested in your program because of its focus on policy analysis and social equity, and because Professor James Chen's research on community benefits agreements speaks directly to what I encountered at DSNI: how legal and financial tools can be structured so that community leverage translates into enforceable commitments rather than goodwill promises developers can quietly abandon. I want to study under him to understand the mechanisms behind agreements like the one I helped negotiate, and to learn how to design policy instruments that hold up under legal and political pressure. Formal training in program evaluation would have helped me determine, with more rigor, whether the BHA's capital repairs actually improved conditions rather than simply making a good headline. Training in political economy would help me understand why housing policy so often stalls at the implementation stage I encountered in Roxbury. Graduate school represents an opportunity to build on the foundation I developed through grassroots work: to translate community knowledge into policy recommendations that hold up to scrutiny, and advocacy strategies that hold up in practice. I believe that strong policy requires both technical skills and authentic engagement with affected communities, which your program cultivates through its field placements and practicum requirements. I am ready to bring my experience to your program, and to keep closing the gap between what policy promises and what it delivers.
feedback2:
Thank you for sharing this draft. You have compelling, substantive experience here, and the raw material for a strong personal statement is clearly present. The main task now is tightening the grammar, sharpening the structure, and making sure every sentence is doing rhetorical work toward convincing an admissions committee that you belong in their program.

Let's start with grammar and mechanics, since these are the most easily fixable issues and matter a great deal in a document meant to showcase your analytical and writing skills. "Policy don't exist in a vacuum" needs subject-verb agreement: either "policy doesn't" or "policies don't." Similarly, "housing policies directly affects the daily lives" should be "affect," since "policies" is plural. Later, "These experiences has convinced me" should be "have convinced me." You also have a tense inconsistency: "Prior to my role at the BHA, I was volunteering at a food bank" mixes past progressive with what should probably be simple past ("I volunteered"). Small errors like these are the kind of thing an admissions reader will notice and that undercut the credibility of an application for analytical, policy-focused graduate work, so a careful proofreading pass (or reading the essay aloud) is essential before you submit.

On structure and organization, the essay currently reads as a chronological list of experiences rather than a shaped argument. You move from BHA to "prior to my role at BHA" to DSNI, and the phrase "prior to" signals a flashback that disrupts the flow you'd built. Consider reordering these experiences either strictly chronologically or, better, thematically—grouping them by what each one taught you about the gap between policy design and lived reality, then building toward the DSNI experience as the moment that showed you the tools to close that gap. This would let the paragraph build to a climax instead of listing accomplishments one after another. Right now, transitions like "Additionally" are functional but flat; look for connective language that shows the intellectual relationship between experiences (e.g., "But if my time at the food bank revealed the gap between policy intent and delivery, my work with DSNI showed me what closing that gap could look like").

The opening sentence is serviceable but not memorable. Admissions essays are read in bulk, and a strong personal statement often opens with a concrete scene, image, or moment rather than a summary statement ("During my three years as a community liaison..."). Consider whether there's a specific interview, a resident's story, or a moment in front of the BHA board that could open the essay and immediately ground the reader in the stakes of your work, before you zoom out to the three-year overview. This would also help humanize the "80 interviews" statistic, which currently risks feeling like a résumé line rather than a lived experience.

In terms of content and paragraph construction, the first paragraph is doing a lot of work—covering BHA, the food bank, and DSNI—and as a result each experience gets compressed into a sentence or two without much reflection. Admissions committees want to see not just what you did but how you think. For each experience, consider adding one sentence of genuine analytical reflection: what did the mold and heating failures reveal about how maintenance funding is allocated? What specific mismatch did you observe between SNAP benefits and food bank capacity, and what would you change? These specifics will do more to demonstrate policy-analytic thinking than the accumulation of experiences itself.

The second paragraph is stronger and more focused, and the reference to Professor Chen's research is a good, specific touch that shows you've done your homework—admissions committees appreciate this kind of specificity. However, you could deepen it further by naming a second faculty member, course, or program feature, or by being more precise about what you hope to learn (e.g., a particular methodology, a specific policy area, a research question you want to pursue). Right now the paragraph gestures at "technical skills" and "field placements" somewhat generically; more specificity here would mirror the specificity you brought to your professional experiences and make the fit argument more persuasive.

One significant omission is any statement of what you intend to do after graduate school. Programs want to know not just that you've done meaningful work and that their program fits your interests, but where you're headed—what kind of role, what kind of impact, what problem you want to spend your career addressing. Adding even a sentence about your post-graduate goals (a policy analyst role, a nonprofit leadership position, work in a specific agency) would give the essay a forward-looking arc and a stronger sense of purpose, rather than ending, as it currently does, on the somewhat generic "I'm ready to bring my experience and my commitment...to your program."

Finally, on word choice: phrases like "vulnerable populations" and "structural barriers" are common in policy writing but can read as jargon when used without elaboration. Since you have concrete, specific stories to draw on, you don't need to lean on abstract policy language to establish your credibility—your specifics will do that work more persuasively. Reserve the more technical vocabulary for moments where you're demonstrating a nuanced grasp of a concept (as you do well with "policy intent and implementation") rather than as a general descriptor.

Overall, this is a strong foundation with real, specific, and relevant experience. The revision priorities, in order, should be: fix the grammar errors, restructure the first paragraph so it builds rather than lists, add a touch more analytical reflection to each experience, sharpen the "why this program" section with additional specifics, and add a concluding statement of your future goals. With these changes, the essay will move from a competent account of your experience to a compelling argument for why you, specifically, need this specific program to do the work you're already doing.

# Personal Statement

During one of my first interviews as a community liaison for the Boston Housing Authority, a resident of a Roxbury public housing complex pulled back a strip of wallpaper to show me the black mold spreading beneath it, then pointed to a broken radiator that had left her apartment without heat for three weeks that winter. Over the next three years, I heard variations of her story more than 80 times, documenting maintenance failures, mold problems, and heating outages across aging public housing units. What struck me most was not the disrepair itself but what it revealed: capital repair budgets were allocated reactively, building by building, only after conditions became severe enough to generate complaints, rather than proactively, based on the age and documented history of the housing stock. This showed me how federal and state housing policies affect the daily lives of the families who depend on them, which is why I want to study public policy. Last year, I helped organize a presentation to the BHA board where residents presented their findings directly, and this led to increased funding for capital repairs in three buildings—proof that policy change often depends on translating lived experience into the kind of evidence institutions are built to respond to.

Before I saw this dynamic at the BHA, I had already encountered a similar disconnect at a local food bank, where I volunteered for two years. There I learned that SNAP benefit calculations often assumed access to fresh food that many recipients' neighborhoods simply didn't have, while food banks themselves were frequently stocked with whatever shelf-stable donations were easiest to collect, not the fresh produce and proteins clients actually needed. The mismatch wasn't a failure of any single actor but a gap between how the benefit was designed and how it was delivered on the ground—the disconnect between policy intent and implementation became clear to me during those years.

But if my time at the food bank revealed the gap between policy intent and delivery, my work with the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative's community benefits agreement negotiations showed me what closing that gap could look like. There, I watched residents use a formal policy tool—the community benefits agreement—to ensure that new development in their neighborhood would benefit existing residents rather than displace them. Together, these experiences have convinced me that I need formal training in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy to understand and address the barriers my community faces.

I am particularly interested in your program because of its focus on policy analysis and social equity, and because Professor James Chen's research on community benefits agreements directly connects to my work at DSNI. I'm also drawn to the program's coursework in quasi-experimental program evaluation methods, which would let me build the quantitative skills I need to assess whether tools like community benefits agreements actually deliver on their promises at scale, particularly in affordable housing finance. Graduate school represents an opportunity for me to deepen my understanding of how to translate community knowledge into effective policy recommendations and advocacy strategies, building on the foundation I've developed through grassroots work. I believe that strong policy requires both technical skills and authentic engagement with affected communities, which your program seems to cultivate through its field placements and practicum requirements.

I'm ready to bring my experience and my commitment to public housing and community development to your program, and I hope to leave it equipped to work as a policy analyst or program evaluator within a public housing agency or community development nonprofit—translating resident testimony and program data alike into the kind of evidence that can move a board, a legislature, or a funder to act, the way it did in Roxbury and on Dudley Street.

# Personal Statement

During my three years as a community liaison for the Boston Housing Authority, I learned that policy don't exist in a vacuum. I worked with residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to document living conditions in aging public housing units, conducting over 80 interviews about maintenance issues, mold problems, and heating failures during winter months. This experience showed me how federal and state housing policies directly affects the daily lives of vulnerable populations, which is why I want to study public policy. Last year, I helped organize a presentation to the BHA board where residents presented their findings directly, and this led to increased funding for capital repairs in three buildings. Prior to my role at the BHA, I was volunteering at a food bank, which taught me about supply chain issues and how SNAP benefits don't always align with what food banks can actually provide to their clients. The disconnect between policy intent and implementation became clear to me during those years. Additionally, I was involved with the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative's community benefits agreement negotiations, where I observed how marginalized communities can leverage policy tools to ensure that new development benefits existing residents rather than displacing them. These experiences has convinced me that I need formal training in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy to understand the structural barriers that my community faces.

I am particularly interested in your program because of its focus on policy analysis and social equity, and also because Professor James Chen's research on community benefits agreements directly connects to my work at DSNI. Graduate school represents an opportunity for me to deepen my understanding of how to translate community knowledge into effective policy recommendations and advocacy strategies, building on the foundation I've developed through grassroots work. I believe that strong policy requires both technical skills and authentic engagement with affected communities, which your program seems to cultivate through its field placements and practicum requirements. I'm ready to bring my experience and my commitment to public housing and community development to your program.

# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

This is a strong draft with compelling content and real evidence of meaningful work. You've effectively shown rather than told the admissions committee why you're passionate about policy, and your specific examples—the 80 interviews, the board presentation, the community benefits agreement work—ground your narrative in concrete impact. That's exactly what graduate programs want to see. However, there are several issues to address before submission, ranging from grammar to the strategic framing of your narrative.

Let me start with the most important concern: the overall arc of your statement. Right now, you spend most of your first paragraph describing three different experiences (BHA, food bank, DSNI), which can feel scattered. While each experience is valuable, the statement would be stronger if you treated one as your primary narrative and wove the others in as supporting evidence. Consider which experience most directly sparked your interest in formal policy study, and organize accordingly. Currently, it's unclear which moment was transformative, which weakens the emotional logic of the piece.

On grammar and mechanics, you have several subject-verb agreement errors that need attention. In your first sentence, "policy don't exist" should be "policy doesn't exist"—policy is singular. Later, you write "these experiences has convinced me," but "experiences" is plural, so it should be "have convinced me." These errors stand out in a graduate application where precision matters, especially for a policy program. Additionally, watch your pronoun references. When you write "which is why I want to study public policy," the word "which" is slightly vague—do you mean the disconnect between policy and lives, or the direct impact you observed? Clarifying this will strengthen the logic.

Your second paragraph has some awkward phrasing that distances you from your own narrative. You say the program "seems to cultivate" certain things—but you could express more conviction here. If you've researched the program carefully, you know rather than suspect what it cultivates. Similarly, "I'm ready to bring my experience...to your program" is a weak closing that shifts focus to what you'll give rather than what you'll achieve. Consider ending with what you hope to accomplish or become through the program, which is more compelling to admissions committees.

There's also a subtle structural issue: your second paragraph pivots to the program itself, but it does so somewhat abruptly and feels disconnected from the rich detail of your first paragraph. You mention Professor Chen specifically, which is excellent, but you might strengthen this connection by briefly explaining why his work matters to your thinking, not just that it connects to your experience. Show the intellectual thread.

One more word choice note: you use the phrase "my community" twice, which is good for establishing investment, but it's not entirely clear which community you're primarily referring to—residents of public housing, marginalized communities more broadly, or your neighborhood? Sharpening this language will make your statement more focused.

Overall, this is well above average for a personal statement. With revision focused on tightening grammar, clarifying your primary narrative arc, and deepening the intellectual engagement in your second paragraph, this will be a strong submission.

# Personal Statement

During my three years as a community liaison for the Boston Housing Authority, I learned that policy doesn't exist in a vacuum. Working with residents in the Roxbury neighborhood, I documented living conditions in aging public housing units, conducting over 80 interviews about maintenance issues, mold problems, and heating failures during winter months. Hearing residents describe the gap between what federal and state housing policies promised and what they actually experienced in their daily lives is what convinced me to pursue formal study in public policy. Last year, I helped organize a presentation to the BHA board where residents shared their findings directly, and this advocacy led to increased funding for capital repairs in three buildings—proof that community voice, translated effectively, can move policy outcomes.

This pattern—the disconnect between policy intent and lived reality, and the power of community voice to close that gap—echoed in other work I did before and during my time at BHA. Earlier, volunteering at a food bank, I saw how supply chain issues and misaligned SNAP benefit structures left clients without the food they needed, even when policy on paper suggested they should have access. And through my involvement with the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative's community benefits agreement negotiations, I watched marginalized communities in Roxbury leverage policy tools to ensure that new development benefited existing residents rather than displacing them. Together, these experiences have convinced me that I need formal training in policy analysis, program evaluation, and political economy to understand the structural barriers facing Roxbury's public housing residents and communities like it.

My work with DSNI is why I am particularly drawn to your program: Professor James Chen's research on community benefits agreements speaks directly to questions I encountered on the ground—how communities can structure agreements that hold developers accountable over time, and what makes some negotiations more durable than others. I want to study under someone who has thought rigorously about the mechanisms I only observed in practice, so that I can understand not just what worked in Roxbury, but why, and how those lessons might generalize elsewhere. Graduate school represents an opportunity for me to deepen my understanding of how to translate community knowledge into effective policy recommendations and advocacy strategies, building on the foundation I've developed through grassroots work. I believe that strong policy requires both technical skills and authentic engagement with affected communities, and your program's field placements and practicum requirements are built to cultivate exactly that combination. I hope to leave your program equipped to design and evaluate policies that give communities like Roxbury's the tools to shape their own futures.
feedback2:
This is a strong foundation with genuinely compelling material—you have specific, substantive experiences that most applicants lack, and the throughline about grassroots knowledge informing policy is exactly the kind of narrative that makes admissions committees sit up. But right now the passage buries its best material under structural and mechanical issues, so let's work through those.

Start with the grammar errors, because they're the first thing a reader notices and they undercut your credibility on a document about precision and analysis. "Policy don't exist" should be "policies don't exist" or "policy does not exist"—watch subject-verb agreement throughout. "How federal and state housing policies directly affects" has the same problem; policies is plural, so it should be "affect." "These experiences has convinced me" should be "have convinced me." These are the kinds of errors that a careful proofread or a read-aloud pass will catch, and given that this is a competitive application, you cannot afford to have them slip through.

The bigger structural issue is chronology and organization. You tell us in paragraph one that you spent three years at BHA, then say "prior to my role at BHA, I was volunteering at a food bank," which retroactively reorders the timeline and creates confusion about what came first and how these experiences build on each other. Right now the paragraph reads as a list of four experiences (BHA, food bank, DSNI, and back to a synthesizing claim about needing formal training) rather than a narrative arc. Consider reordering chronologically, or better yet, organizing thematically around the throughline you already gestured at: each experience taught you something distinct about the gap between policy design and policy implementation, and you want that argument to build rather than just accumulate. Right now the food bank experience and the DSNI experience each get only a sentence or two, which makes them feel like a list of bullet points translated into prose rather than developed anecdotes. If you don't have room to develop all three experiences with real specificity, consider cutting one (the food bank material is the least connected to your public housing/community development throughline) so you can give more depth to the other two.

Related to this: the BHA paragraph is doing far more work than the others, with the vivid detail (80 interviews, mold, heating failures, the board presentation and its funding outcome) that graduate admissions readers want. That specificity is what makes a personal statement land—so ask yourself whether the DSNI experience deserves similarly concrete detail. What did you actually do in those negotiations? What was the outcome? Right now it's described only in the abstract ("observed how marginalized communities can leverage policy tools"), and abstraction is much less persuasive than the granular detail you gave for BHA.

The first paragraph also tries to do too much at once—it introduces three separate work experiences and also announces your interest in public policy and your conclusion about needing formal training, all in a single paragraph with no clear internal structure. Consider breaking this into two paragraphs: one that narrates the BHA experience with its concrete outcome, and a second that handles the food bank and/or DSNI material, with a clearer transition sentence between them so the reader understands why you're moving from one experience to the next rather than feeling like you're reading a résumé narrated in prose.

On word choice: "vulnerable populations" and "structural barriers" are fine but slightly generic policy-speak; since you have such concrete, textured material (mold, heating failures, SNAP mismatches), lean into that specificity rather than retreating to abstraction when you summarize. Similarly, "authentic engagement" and "translate community knowledge into effective policy recommendations" are serviceable phrases, but they're the kind of language every applicant to a policy program uses—if you can find one moment or fact that shows this rather than states it, the essay will feel more distinctive.

The second paragraph, which addresses why this specific program, is actually well-constructed and does what it needs to do: it names a specific professor and connects his research to your own experience, which is exactly the kind of specificity admissions committees want, and it ties the program's field placements back to your stated belief about technical skill plus community engagement. This paragraph could serve as a model for tightening the first: notice how efficiently it moves from claim to specific evidence (Professor Chen, field placements) without excess narration.

Finally, think about your ending. "I'm ready to bring my experience and my commitment to public housing and community development to your program" is a serviceable closing line, but it's fairly generic and doesn't leave the reader with a distinctive final image or claim. Given how strong your concrete material is elsewhere (the 80 interviews, the board presentation, the funding outcome), consider closing with something that gestures forward to what you specifically want to do with this training—a sentence that shows you've thought about your post-graduate trajectory, not just your motivation for applying. That will leave the reader with forward momentum rather than a general statement of enthusiasm.

Overall: fix the subject-verb agreement errors, resolve the chronological confusion in paragraph one, decide whether to cut or develop the food bank material, add concrete detail to the DSNI anecdote, and consider splitting your dense first paragraph into two with a clear transition. The content and voice here are already good—this is a matter of tightening structure and mechanics so the strength of your experience comes through clearly.

# Graduate School Personal Statement – Molecular Biology

My interest in molecular biology begin during my junior year at State University when I take a cell signaling course with Professor Martinez. We was studying the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and I become fascinated by how a single protein interaction can cascade into complex developmental outcomes. That same semester, I joined Dr. Sarah Chen's lab to investigate how mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene disrupt normal signaling in colorectal cancer cells. My work involves using CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce specific mutations and then analyze the resulting changes in protein localization through immunofluorescence microscopy. The experience of designing my own experiments, troubleshooting when my transfections failed repeatedly, and eventually generating meaningful data have showed me that research is what I want to pursue. Additionally, I was also involved in the undergraduate research symposium where I presented my findings on APC mutations, which were well-received by faculty members. I am committed to understanding how molecular mechanisms drive disease progression, particularly in cancer biology.

Graduate school represent the next logical step in my development as a scientist because I want to deepen my expertise and contribute to novel discoveries about protein-protein interactions in oncogenic pathways. Beyond my lab work, I also tutored general chemistry students at the university tutoring center, which helps me develop communication skills and reinforce fundamental concepts. My experience in Dr. Chen's lab has prepared me well for the rigor of graduate-level research. I read extensively about recent developments in the field, including the work on synthetic lethal interactions in BRCA-mutant cancers, and I believe your program's focus on structural biology and drug design align well with my goals of eventually developing targeted therapeutics. The combination of my technical skills in molecular techniques, my passion for understanding cancer biology, and my dedication to scientific inquiry makes me a strong candidate for your program.

feedback1:
This is a strong foundation for a personal statement — you have genuine, specific research experience (named mentors, named genes and pathways, real techniques like CRISPR-Cas9 and immunofluorescence), and the whole piece stays tightly focused on your development as a scientist without ever drifting into irrelevant territory. That specificity and topical discipline are exactly what this genre rewards, so don't lose them as you revise. The most urgent work now is less about content and more about polish and argumentative sharpness.

Start with a careful line edit for verb tense and agreement — this is the most mechanical issue, but also the most important to fix, because errors like "begin," "take," "we was," "I become," "Graduate school represent," and "focus...align" recur throughout and are the kind of thing an admissions reader will notice immediately. The essay drifts between past tense for your undergraduate narrative and present tense for your current beliefs, and while some of that shift is appropriate (e.g., ongoing habits like "I am committed to" or "I read extensively"), you should go sentence by sentence and confirm each verb matches whether you're describing something completed or something ongoing. In a science-focused application, precision in grammar reads as precision in thought, so this is worth a dedicated pass on its own.

Once the grammar is clean, focus on tightening the argument itself. Two things would strengthen it most: first, make your "fit" case concrete. Right now the connection to the program is a single passing mention of "structural biology and drug design," which could apply to almost any program with that focus — naming a specific faculty member, lab, or resource that connects to your interest in protein-protein interactions would make this argument land. Second, cash out your research narrative with an actual result. You set up real stakes (troubleshooting failed transfections, presenting at a symposium) but resolve them with vague phrases like "generating meaningful data" or "well-received by faculty" — telling the reader what you actually found, even briefly, would let your work speak for itself rather than asking the reader to take your word for its significance. Along the same lines, the tutoring sentence currently feels dropped in without connecting to your research goals; either give it a clear purpose (e.g., tying it to an interest in teaching or mentoring in graduate school) or cut it, and consider pairing it with the symposium mention as a second "other experiences" beat rather than leaving it stranded mid-argument. Finally, watch for redundancy at the ends of both paragraphs — each closes with a similar restatement of your commitment to cancer biology, and the very last line ("makes me a strong candidate") summarizes rather than advances your case. Trimming one of these restatements and replacing the final sentence with a forward-looking, specific research question you'd want to pursue in the program would leave a much stronger final impression.

At the structural level, these same fixes would also resolve most of what's holding the essay back: consider opening with a brief framing sentence that states your overall goal before diving into the origin story, and consider splitting the second paragraph into two clearer movements — one on why graduate school in general, one on why this specific program — so the piece builds toward a real conclusion rather than circling back to the same claim twice. Varying sentence length would help too; nearly every sentence in both paragraphs is a long, multi-clause construction, and a few shorter, more direct sentences placed deliberately would give your key points more room to land.

Last, once the structural and argumentative issues are addressed, do a pass for word choice. Your technical vocabulary is genuinely strong and signals real fluency in the field, but some of the connective and evaluative language leans on personal-statement stock phrases — "next logical step in my development," "align well with my goals," "strong candidate for your program" — that undercut the more specific, technical voice you use elsewhere. Replacing these with more active, precise phrasing (and trimming small redundancies like "Additionally... also") will make the polished, technical parts of the essay stand out even more.

# Graduate School Personal Statement – Molecular Biology

My goal is to become a cancer biologist who uses mechanistic insight into protein-protein interactions to develop targeted therapeutics. That goal began during my junior year at State University, when I took a cell signaling course with Professor Martinez. We studied the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and I became fascinated by how a single protein interaction can cascade into complex developmental outcomes. That same semester, I joined Dr. Sarah Chen's lab to investigate how mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene disrupt normal signaling in colorectal cancer cells. My work involved using CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce specific mutations and then analyzing the resulting changes in protein localization through immunofluorescence microscopy. I designed my own experiments, troubleshot repeated transfection failures, and eventually found that APC mutants lacking the β-catenin-binding domain caused β-catenin to accumulate in the nucleus rather than remain sequestered in the cytoplasm. That result showed me research is what I want to pursue.

Graduate school is the setting where I can deepen this expertise and contribute new discoveries about protein-protein interactions in oncogenic pathways. My time in Dr. Chen's lab prepared me for that kind of independent, sustained inquiry, and I have continued to read about developments in the field, including work on synthetic lethal interactions in BRCA-mutant cancers, to understand how mechanistic findings like mine translate into therapeutic strategies.

Your program is the right place for that work because of its focus on structural biology and drug design, particularly Dr. [Faculty Name]'s work using cryo-EM to resolve the destruction complex that regulates β-catenin degradation. That structural approach is exactly what my own cell-based work lacks, and combining the two would let me ask not just whether a mutation disrupts signaling, but how it does so at the molecular level. I also presented my APC findings at the undergraduate research symposium and tutored general chemistry students at the university tutoring center, experiences that sharpened my ability to explain complex mechanisms clearly to different audiences. I want to spend graduate school asking a specific question: how do structural changes in APC-β-catenin binding alter the kinetics of destruction complex assembly, and can that mechanism be exploited therapeutically?

# Feedback on Your Graduate School Personal Statement

Your statement demonstrates solid understanding of molecular biology concepts and shows genuine engagement with research, which are important foundations for a strong application. However, there are several areas where revision will significantly strengthen your writing and make a more compelling case for your candidacy.

Let me start with grammar and mechanics, since these errors distract readers and can undermine your credibility in an academic context. You have multiple subject-verb agreement errors that need immediate correction: "My interest in molecular biology begin" should use "begins," "We was studying" should be "We were studying," and "Graduate school represent" should be "represents." Additionally, "I become fascinated" should be "I became fascinated" to maintain consistent past tense throughout your narrative. These are basic errors that suggest insufficient proofreading, and graduate admissions committees will notice them. I'd strongly recommend reading your statement aloud slowly and having at least one peer review it before submission.

Beyond mechanics, your word choices sometimes lack precision. For instance, you write that your experience "have showed me" (which is also grammatically incorrect) that research is what you want to pursue. Consider more sophisticated phrasing: your experience "demonstrated" or "revealed" rather than "showed." Similarly, phrases like "I am committed to understanding" and "makes me a strong candidate" are fairly generic. Graduate admissions essays are strengthened when you use more specific, active language that shows rather than tells the reader about your qualifications.

The larger structural issue is that your statement lacks a clear narrative arc or memorable through-line. Right now, it reads more like a checklist of accomplishments—you did CRISPR work, you presented at a symposium, you tutored, you read recent papers—rather than a cohesive story about your intellectual development. The best personal statements take readers on a journey: they show how you arrived at your research interests, what specific moments crystallized your thinking, and why you're pursuing graduate school now. Your opening about the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is promising because it's a specific entry point, but you don't develop it deeply enough. What exactly about that pathway sparked your curiosity? Was it a particular question that emerged from the course? Did Professor Martinez inspire you in a specific way? These concrete details would make your narrative more engaging and memorable.

Your second paragraph also feels somewhat scattered. You jump from explaining why graduate school is important (deepening expertise) to your tutoring experience to recent literature you've read to your desire to develop therapeutics. While all of these elements are relevant to your candidacy, they're not well integrated. Instead of listing accomplishments, try building paragraphs around central ideas. For example, one paragraph might focus on how your lab experiences have prepared you specifically for graduate-level research; another might address how your broader intellectual interests align with the specific program you're applying to.

On that note, you mention that the program's "focus on structural biology and drug design align well" with your goals, but this feels like a placeholder that could apply to many programs. When you revise, research the specific program deeply and reference particular faculty members, specific labs, or unique facilities that genuinely excite you. Admissions committees can tell when these statements are generic versus genuinely tailored, and specificity matters tremendously.

There's also a subtle issue with tone. Some phrases feel defensive or self-promotional in a way that undermines your voice. "The combination of my technical skills in molecular techniques, my passion for understanding cancer biology, and my dedication to scientific inquiry makes me a strong candidate for your program" is the kind of statement that weakens rather than strengthens your application. You don't need to explicitly claim you're a strong candidate; instead, let your experiences and thoughtful reflection demonstrate your qualifications.

Finally, consider what's missing. You mention troubleshooting when transfections failed, which is actually a much more interesting and humanizing detail than many of your other points. What did you learn from those failures? How did they shape your approach to experimental design? Graduate students need resilience and adaptability, and these kinds of reflective moments reveal character in ways that listing accomplishments cannot. Your statement would be more powerful if it spent less time cataloging what you've done and more time reflecting on what you've learned and how those lessons have shaped your understanding of yourself as a scientist.

In summary: fix all grammatical errors immediately, develop your narrative with more concrete detail and reflection rather than listing accomplishments, ensure your paragraphs are organized around central ideas rather than scattered observations, and tailor your statement more specifically to the program. Most importantly, let readers see your thinking and your growth, not just your resume in paragraph form.

# Graduate School Personal Statement – Molecular Biology

My interest in molecular biology begins during my junior year at State University when I took a cell signaling course with Professor Martinez. We were studying the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and I remember sitting in class the day Professor Martinez described how a single misfolded protein could tip an entire developmental program off course. I found myself wondering what would happen if that same logic applied not to development but to disease—what if the same delicate cascade that builds an embryo could, when broken, build a tumor instead? That question stayed with me long after the semester ended, and it led me to join Dr. Sarah Chen's lab that same term to investigate how mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene disrupt normal signaling in colorectal cancer cells. My work involves using CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce specific mutations and then analyzing the resulting changes in protein localization through immunofluorescence microscopy.

The road to generating meaningful data was not straightforward. My transfections failed repeatedly during my first few months in the lab, and I spent weeks troubleshooting variables I had initially overlooked—cell confluency, reagent freshness, even the timing of media changes. Those failures were frustrating, but they taught me to think more rigorously about experimental design and to treat a negative result as information rather than defeat. When I finally saw consistent, interpretable localization patterns, I understood that this kind of patient, iterative problem-solving was exactly what I wanted to spend my career doing. I later presented these findings on APC mutations at our undergraduate research symposium, where the questions I received from faculty pushed me to think more critically about the broader implications of my data for colorectal cancer progression.

My time in Dr. Chen's lab has prepared me for graduate-level research in ways that go beyond technical proficiency. Designing my own experiments and defending my interpretations to Dr. Chen taught me to think like an independent investigator rather than simply follow a protocol. Graduate school represents the next logical step in my development as a scientist because it will allow me to deepen this kind of independent inquiry and contribute new insight into protein-protein interactions in oncogenic pathways.

My scientific thinking has also been shaped outside the lab. Tutoring general chemistry students at the university tutoring center forced me to explain fundamental concepts clearly and patiently, a skill I now recognize as essential to communicating research effectively—whether to a struggling student or to a room of scientists. I have also followed recent developments in the field, including work on synthetic lethal interactions in BRCA-mutant cancers, which has sharpened my interest in how structural understanding of protein interactions can inform targeted therapeutic design. This is part of why I am drawn to your program: Dr. [Faculty Name]'s work using cryo-EM to resolve the structural basis of oncogenic complex formation speaks directly to the questions I began asking in Professor Martinez's classroom, and I would welcome the opportunity to bring my background in CRISPR-based functional studies into a structural biology setting.

I am drawn to graduate study because I want to keep asking the kind of question that first hooked me in that cell signaling course—not just how a pathway works, but what happens when it breaks, and how that knowledge might one day inform a therapy. I look forward to bringing that curiosity, along with the resilience I built through months of failed transfections, into your program.

# Feedback on Your Graduate School Personal Statement

Let me start with what's working well: your statement has a clear narrative arc that shows genuine intellectual development, and your specific examples—the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, your CRISPR work, the immunofluorescence microscopy—demonstrate real engagement with molecular biology research. Your passion for understanding disease mechanisms comes through authentically, and you've made a genuine effort to connect your experiences to your future goals. These are important strengths in a personal statement.

However, there are several areas where revisions would significantly strengthen your application. I'll address the most impactful issues first.

**Grammar and Subject-Verb Agreement**

Your statement contains multiple grammatical errors that, while individually small, collectively distract from your credibility as a scholar. In your opening sentence, "My interest in molecular biology begin" should use "began" to match the past tense of the sentence and your subject. Similarly, "We was studying" should be "We were studying." Later, you write "I become fascinated," which breaks tense consistency—this should be "became." In the second paragraph, "Graduate school represent" needs to be "represents." These errors suggest the statement wasn't carefully proofread, which raises questions about your attention to detail in scientific work. Before final submission, read through slowly, checking that every verb agrees with its subject and maintains appropriate tense throughout.

**Wordiness and Redundancy**

Your second paragraph bogs down with unnecessary phrases that don't add substance. You write "Additionally, I was also involved in the undergraduate research symposium"—the "Additionally" and "was also" are redundant; choose one. More significantly, the sentence about tutoring chemistry ("Beyond my lab work, I also tutored general chemistry students...") feels disconnected from your main narrative. While it demonstrates communication skills, which is valuable, this sentence interrupts your flow just as you're building toward your research interests and career goals. Consider whether this detail is essential, or whether it dilutes your focus on what makes you a compelling researcher.

The closing sentence—"The combination of my technical skills in molecular techniques, my passion for understanding cancer biology, and my dedication to scientific inquiry makes me a strong candidate for your program"—is generic language that could apply to many applicants. Admissions committees expect this; you don't need to state it. Use that space instead to deepen a more unique insight about your research vision.

**Showing Rather Than Telling**

Related to the above, you often *tell* the reader what you've learned rather than *showing* it. You state, "The experience of designing my own experiments, troubleshooting when my transfections failed repeatedly, and eventually generating meaningful data have showed me that research is what I want to pursue." This is somewhat generic. Instead, consider: What specifically did you learn from that troubleshooting? Did a failed transfection lead you to an unexpected discovery? Did it teach you something about experimental design that changed your thinking? The vivid detail of "transfections failed repeatedly" is great, but you should zoom in on *why this matters* rather than announcing that it showed you your passion. Your readers are trained to recognize genuine passion from specific details—you don't need to declare it.

**Paragraph Structure and Flow**

Your two paragraphs serve different purposes, but they could be better integrated. The first paragraph is essentially "here's what sparked my interest and here's my lab experience." The second shifts to "here's why grad school is next and here's what I'm interested in." While this isn't wrong structurally, there's an opportunity to create a more cohesive narrative. Consider whether you could weave your description of what you want to achieve (understanding protein-protein interactions, developing therapeutics) more explicitly into your first paragraph, so that your second paragraph builds on that foundation rather than introducing new ideas. Right now, the statement reads a bit like two separate thoughts rather than one unified argument.

**Specificity and Program Alignment**

You mention that the program's focus on "structural biology and drug design align well with my goals," which is good—you're showing you've researched the program. However, this is quite brief. Graduate admissions committees want to see that you've genuinely considered *why this specific program*, not just that it has the right keywords. Do you know of particular faculty members whose work excites you? Have you reviewed their recent publications? Can you name specific courses or resources? Even one additional sentence showing deeper knowledge of the program would strengthen this section considerably.

**Voice and Authenticity**

On a more subtle level, your statement occasionally sounds like you're writing what you think admissions committees want to hear, rather than in your own voice. Phrases like "deepen my expertise," "the next logical step in my development," and "strong candidate for your program" sound rehearsed. Personal statements typically have word limits. If this is meant to be concise (under 500-750 words, as many are), you should cut the tutoring sentence and possibly trim some of the redundancy. # Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Your personal statement demonstrates genuine intellectual curiosity and a clear commitment to comparative literature. You've selected compelling anecdotes and provided specific examples of your scholarly work, both of which are strengths. However, there are several areas where revision would significantly strengthen your application.

Let me start with the most urgent issue: sentence-level mechanics. Your passage contains multiple comma splices that undermine your credibility as a serious writer, particularly problematic in a graduate application where grammatical precision signals academic rigor. In your first paragraph, "it made me realize" should follow a period or semicolon after *Norwegian Wood*, not a comma. Similarly, "I had never considered" creates another splice after "American authors," and "I became fascinated" after your Tokyo bookstore visit needs punctuation revision. The phrase "it's about understanding" in your final sentence of the first paragraph should be "it is" in formal academic writing. These aren't minor quibbles—grammar matters enormously in graduate admissions because it demonstrates your ability to communicate clearly in academic contexts.

Beyond mechanics, I'd encourage you to reconsider your paragraph structure and emphasis. Right now, your first paragraph spends considerable energy on the origin story of your interest (Murakami, the dorm room realization, Professor Chen's seminar), but this takes up valuable space that might be better allocated to demonstrating your actual scholarly capabilities. Graduate programs care less about the moment you "realized" something and more about what you've done with that realization. Your Tokyo summer and visits to bookstores, while charming, feel somewhat tangential to your main intellectual project. Consider condensing or eliminating some of these early anecdotes so you can give more weight to your actual research and academic contributions.

Your second paragraph is much stronger because it foregrounds your substantive work—your honors thesis and translation collective involvement. This is where you should linger, because these examples directly demonstrate your ability to do graduate-level work. However, even here, I'd suggest deepening your analysis. You tell us that you "argued that while both texts use fantastical elements to engage with postcolonial trauma, their narrative structures reflect distinct cultural approaches to time and causality," but you don't actually explain *how* or *why* their approaches differ. What specifically did you discover about García Márquez versus Tutuola? A sentence or two of substantive detail would be far more persuasive than mentioning you received an A. Similarly, with your translation work, you identify the challenge of "preserving tone and wordplay," but what have you learned about *solving* this problem? What specific translation choices have you grappled with?

I also notice a tonal inconsistency in how you discuss your work. Phrases like "the most rewarding intellectual work I have done" and "I believe this program would allow me" feel somewhat informal and self-congratulatory for academic writing. Rather than telling the reader how rewarding your work was, show them through the intellectual substance of what you discovered. # Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Your personal statement demonstrates genuine intellectual engagement with comparative literature and shows real self-awareness about your scholarly development. You've chosen meaningful examples and reveal authentic passion for your subject. However, there are several areas where you can significantly strengthen this piece, particularly in structure, mechanics, and strategic positioning for a graduate school application.

Let me start with the most critical issue: this passage needs clearer organizational logic and more strategic emphasis. Right now, you're covering a lot of ground—your initial inspiration, coursework, a summer abroad, your thesis, and your current involvement—but the progression feels somewhat scattered. For a graduate school application, you want to guide the reader toward a clear intellectual trajectory and a compelling reason why this particular program is right for you. Consider restructuring so that your experiences build toward your current research interests and future goals more explicitly. The opening anecdote about Murakami is engaging, but it takes up significant real estate without advancing your argument much beyond "I became interested in comparative literature." You might compress this inspiration into a sentence or two and use that space to develop your more recent and substantive work.

On grammar and mechanics, you have two run-on sentences that need attention. In your first paragraph, "My interest in comparative literature began when I was reading Haruki Murakami's *Norwegian Wood* in my dorm room during freshman year, it made me realize..." is a comma splice. Similarly, later in that paragraph: "I had grown up in suburban Ohio reading mostly American authors, I had never considered..." and "I visited independent bookstores and literary museums, I became fascinated..." all connect independent clauses with commas. These should be separated into distinct sentences or restructured with appropriate conjunctions or punctuation. These errors stand out because they appear repeatedly and suggest carelessness in proofreading.

Your word choice is generally strong, but there are moments where you could be more precise or less repetitive. You use "experience" or "experiences" three times in the first paragraph, and "literature" appears frequently throughout without variation (you might sometimes say "literary analysis," "texts," or "narrative traditions"). More importantly, you say "this experience was transformative for my understanding of literature" after discussing the seminar, which is somewhat vague. What specifically transformed? The second paragraph is denser and more accomplishment-heavy, which is good, but it again tries to accomplish too much. You move from your thesis to the translation collective to your fit with the program in quick succession. Each of these could be its own moment of emphasis. # Personal Statement

During my senior capstone, my design group built a hydraulic prosthetic ankle for amputees, one that could adjust its response depending on whether a patient was walking slowly, quickly, or on uneven ground. One afternoon at the prosthetics clinic downtown, a patient testing an early prototype told us that the ankle felt sluggish when she tried to catch herself on a curb—a small comment that sent us back to the lab to rework the valve timing in the hydraulic circuit. That moment stayed with me: a single piece of feedback, delivered by someone whose daily mobility depended on our design choices, reshaped weeks of engineering work. I spent three months running MATLAB simulations of the fluid dynamics and testing prototypes against exactly this kind of real-world input. The feedback from clinic patients was invaluable, not because it was always technically precise, but because it forced us to translate lived experience into design specifications. Watching that translation happen—hearing "it feels sluggish" become "increase the orifice diameter by 0.5mm"—taught me that engineering problems have real human consequences, and that precision and iteration matter most when someone is depending on the result.

After the capstone ended, I continued working on the project through the summer, refining the valve design and running additional trials with the clinic. That experience clarified what I want to do in graduate school: pursue research in assistive device design and rehabilitation engineering, with a focus on fluid power systems that can adapt in real time to a user's movement. I want to design prosthetic and orthotic devices that respond as naturally as possible to the people who rely on them.

My interest in mechanical engineering began earlier, during my junior year, when I joined the design team for our school's solar car project. Building a car for a national competition meant balancing constraints that often worked against each other: reducing drag meant reshaping the body in ways that complicated weight distribution, and maximizing solar cell efficiency meant fighting for surface area that the aerodynamic design wanted to eliminate. Resolving those competing demands, and watching the finished car perform on the track, gave me my first real sense of what mechanical engineering could accomplish. I learned to use SolidWorks to model the chassis and suspension components, and I learned—less comfortably—how to manage conflict among twelve teammates split across electrical, mechanical, and body subteams. When our electrical lead and body-panel lead disagreed for a week over how to route wiring without compromising the shell's aerodynamics, I found myself mediating between them, translating each side's constraints into terms the other could act on. That conflict showed me that solving engineering problems as part of a team requires as much communication skill as technical skill, a lesson I carried directly into the more collaborative environment of my capstone.

These two experiences—one that gave me technical range, one that gave me purpose—are why I am applying to your mechanical engineering program specifically. I am especially interested in Professor [Name]'s work on adaptive fluid power systems and in the opportunities for hands-on prototyping in the [Lab Name]. I would like to pursue a thesis that extends the valve-control work from my capstone into a more general adaptive control scheme for prosthetic and orthotic devices, and I hope to take coursework in advanced fluid mechanics and biomechanics to support that research. Longer-term, I want to contribute to the field of rehabilitation engineering by developing assistive devices that are both mechanically robust and responsive to the individual patients who use them. Your program's combination of strength in fluid power systems and its connections to clinical partners makes it, I believe, the right place for me to pursue that goal.
